about: The versions of the cell, oldest first. Written by tools/evolution/add.sh and by hand for the history; read by //:scorecard_test, //:versions_test and tools/evolution/pages.py. docs/scorecard.md explains every field.

directions.title: A stand-in cell: one KUKA arm picking modules in physics
directions.description: One KUKA KR 210 arm with a suction tool picks solar modules from a tilted pallet and sets them on a torque tube that a conveyor steps along, all in MuJoCo physics. Perception, motion planning and control are written in C++ for it. A depth camera finds the front module, a planned carry takes it to the other side, and a second camera checks how the module sits on the tool and corrects the placement. A gate in the tests runs whole pallets with randomized offsets and fails if a module lands out of tolerance. Its figures are measured in simulation runs.
directions.limits: It is another cell: ten slots of a square tube, not the real parts of a bay. The simulation is kinder than a real cell: the grip never slips, the module is rigid, and the motor and camera noise figures are estimates.

directions.title: One 40 ft base: the cell on the real parts
directions.description: The cell is rebuilt on the real parts of a tracker bay, a round torque tube, rails, modules and their fastenings, on one 40 ft base. In run 011 the base is a container with both long sides open; it later becomes a flat rack. The work is kinematic: layouts are written as data and checked by a program for transport, reach, clearance, load, the ways in and out, and time. The figures are planned or come from a time model, and no controller or cycle runs in physics yet.
directions.limits: The base may carry 13,608 kg in transit (30,000 lb), and the arms, tracks, tools and bay have to fit within it. Times come from a time model, not from a run in physics.

directions.title: Two 20 ft flat racks side by side
directions.description:
Two 20 ft flat racks stand side by side on their long sides, about 25 mm apart. Each has its own transport limit of 13,608 kg (30,000 lb) and is structurally separate, but the two work as one cell and arms may reach across the gap. The torque tube is worked in sections, because a tube of 30 ft or more does not fit whole. Units at the infeed and the outfeed stage the tube. The cell of this direction is described and checked in [docs/two-flat-racks-cell.md](../two-flat-racks-cell.md): two layouts, `two_flat_racks_2_pin_arms` and `two_flat_racks_1_pin_arm`, each worked in three stages and passing every row of the checker.

![two_flat_racks_2_pin_arms, finished bay at the last stage](../img/two_flat_racks_2_pin_arms.png)

![two_flat_racks_1_pin_arm, finished bay at the last stage](../img/two_flat_racks_1_pin_arm.png)
directions.limits: Each rack carries at most 13,608 kg (30,000 lb) in transit, so the mass of the cell has to be split between them. The tube is worked in three stages; its two transfers in a bay take 30 s each, a figure of the layout, not the model of a move. Times come from a time model, not from a run in physics.

versions.title: A blind pick and place
versions.changed: The first cell: a KUKA KR 210 arm with a suction tool, a tilted pallet of 30 modules, a conveyor with a torque tube, and one depth camera. The cycle runs from a script that assumes the pallet is exactly where the drawing says.
versions.why: To have a whole cycle running in physics, scored by placement error and cycle time, before any perception was added.

recording_source.shows: The same offset pallet without and with the camera; blind, the tool meets the glass 9 mm early and the cycle stops.

versions.title: The check after pickup corrects the placement
versions.changed: With `--check` the planned carry passes over a second depth camera looking up. The arm holds still, the camera finds the module's underside, and the set-down is corrected so that the module, not the tool, lands on the slot. The carry is planned and the cycle can use it with `--carry planned`.
versions.why: A camera calibration that is off is frozen in at the grip and goes straight into the placement, and the script cannot see that error.

recording_source.shows: The second module held over the check camera, then set down beside the first.

versions.title: Whole pallets in tolerance: the gate
versions.changed: A test, the gate, runs eight whole pallets of 30 modules with the planned carry and the check, with noisy pictures and both cameras' calibrations off by 1 mm and 0.05 degrees. It fails if any module is not placed or lands more than 3 mm or 0.15 degrees from its slot, and it saves every failure with the command that reruns it.
versions.why: Single trials had shown the cycle worked, but nothing stopped a later change from breaking it, so whole pallets in tolerance became a condition of the tests.

versions.title: The real parts of a bay and the container, as models
versions.changed: The real parts of one bay of a single-axis tracker, after Nextracker's NX Horizon, are written down in docs/bay-hardware.md and built as models: a round torque tube with 11 rails, 10 modules and 51 fastening points. A 40 ft container with both long sides open is modelled with the figures that decide whether a bay fits and passes out. The cell itself does not change and still uses its old square tube.
versions.why: The stand-in cell used a square tube and ten slots, so the next step needed the real parts of a bay and a container to work in, with each figure marked published, derived or ours.

recording_source.shows: The 40 ft container in its working state with a bay passing out through one open side.

versions.title: A bay of nine modules and a checked layout in a 40 ft container
versions.changed: A bay becomes nine modules and ten rails, so the section is 10.616 m long with 46 fastenings. A layout is one JSON file, and a program checks it for transport, reach, clearance, load, the ways in and out, and time. Five layouts are compared in docs/layout.md and below_rails_by_module_arm is chosen: a KUKA KR 210 on a track sets rails and modules, and a UR10e on a floor track bolts, locates and pins.
versions.why: The container could not take a bay of ten modules with room to work, and the cell needed a layout whose reach, clearance and load were checked before anything was built.

recording_source.shows: The chosen layout with a finished bay on the tube, both arms waiting inside the container.

versions.title: Three pin arms on the flat rack: a whole bay planned
versions.changed: The cell stands on the base of a 40 ft flat rack: one KUKA KR 210 on a track sets the ten rails and nine modules, and three UR10e on tracks below the bay drive the strap bolts and locate, pin and swage the modules. Every move of every arm for one bay is planned free of collision, the four arms are scheduled on one clock, and the plan is verified and committed.
versions.why: The owner allowed the first cell to stand on a flat rack with up to three pin arms. Of one, two and three pin arms, three gave the shortest planned bay, 644.28 s against 700.08 s and 907.34 s, with the same tightest clearance at a pose.

rehashed.why: The chosen flag left the layout files for versions/versions.json (the newest version with status chosen), so that a later layout can be chosen without changing a registered file. The only change to the layout file is the removed line "chosen"; its plan was made again and is the same but for the layout's sha256, and its scorecard is unchanged but for the two hashes.

The plan now holds three bays back to back, planned and verified (src/layout_bays.h); cycle_s is the three-bay average, (end of bay 2's bay_out - start of bay 0's tube_in) / 3, with one_bay_s and interval_s beside it. Bay 0 is unchanged: one_bay_s is the cycle_s this version had.

versions.title: Three pin arms on the flat rack, the bay shortened by the order of work
versions.changed: The same cell as v09, with no new part, arm or tool and no changed time, speed or margin: only the order of work changed. The modules are set in the order 0, 1, 4, 2, 5, 7, 6, 3, 8, so that the three pin arms' modules come in turn. A module is taken as soon as the strap bolts of its own two rails are driven, not after the last bolt. A pin arm changes to its pin tool and takes its magazine as soon as its bolts are done, not when its first module is set. The planned bay is 560.45 s, down from 644.28 s.
versions.why: The cycle time of a bay is the first measure. Of 23 orders planned in full (tools/order/search.py), this one gave the shortest bay that the verifier passes. Every other measure of the scorecard is unchanged: 0.3849 failures per bay, 39 parts, 4 arms, 40 driven axes, 3,426.3 kg in transit. The least clearance over the schedule is 0.0180 m against 0.015 m.

rehashed.why: The plan now holds three bays back to back, planned and verified (src/layout_bays.h); cycle_s is the three-bay average, (end of bay 2's bay_out - start of bay 0's tube_in) / 3, with one_bay_s and interval_s beside it. Bay 0 is unchanged: one_bay_s is the cycle_s this version had.

versions.title: Two 20 ft flat racks, two pin arms: three bays planned
versions.changed: The first version of the second direction: the cell on two 20 ft flat racks set side by side, one KUKA KR 210 that sets the rails and modules, two pin arms and a bolt arm. The torque tube is worked in three stages that the infeed and outfeed units move through. Three bays are planned whole, 378 of 378 moves, verified and committed: 1003.47 s for one bay and a cycle time of 969.67 s over three.
versions.why: It gives the direction of two 20 ft flat racks its first cycle time measured the same way as v10, so that the two directions can be weighed. At 969.67 s against v10's 554.55 s it is a candidate, not chosen: pin arm B has 28 of the 36 holes and the most work, and every bay stops for two 30 s transfers of the tube.

versions.title: Two 20 ft flat racks, pin arms balanced: three bays planned
versions.changed: Pin arms A and B of v11's cell share the holes by whole modules, A 20 holes and B 16 (before 8 and 28), and pin arm A works each module in one posture and waits in it. Three bays are planned whole, 381 of 381 moves, verified and committed: 852.84 s for one bay and a cycle time of 819.11 s over three.
versions.why: It is the measured step of the direction of two 20 ft flat racks after v11: 819.11 s against v11's 969.67 s, so a candidate weighed against v11. It is still 1.48 times v10's 554.55 s, so v10 stays chosen; the module arm is now the busiest arm, with pin arm A close behind.
